title: Mīzān al-ṣarf
author: anonymous
subject: sarf
summary: Mīzān al-ṣarf, “the scale of ṣarf”, is the short Persian primer with which the Dars-i Niẓāmī of the Indian madrasas begins ṣarf; its author is not known. On the paradigm faʿala yafʿulu it builds, step by step and always by a stated rule, the conjugation of the sound triliteral verb: the past and the muḍāriʿ in their fourteen forms, active and passive, affirmed and negated with mā, lā, lan and lam, with the lām and the two nūns of emphasis, the imperative and the prohibition, and then the two participles, the nouns of place and of instrument, and the elative. The student learns it by heart, table by table. The lessons follow a Kanpur lithograph of 1905, explain in English each rule that the Persian gives, and set out its tables beside the same forms of naṣara from the engine.

lessons.title: The three times, and the past
body: After an Arabic ḥamdala the book turns to the student in Persian, with an Arabic prayer for him: asʿadaka Allāhu taʿālā fī al-dārayni, “may God Most High make you happy in both abodes”. Then its first rule: all the verbs that change their form (afʿāl munṣarifa) are of three kinds, past (māḍī), future (mustaqbal) and present (ḥāl), and “whatever is other than these three branches off from them”. The imperative, the prohibition and the participles, which come later in the book, are all built from these.

The past is “a verb that relates to past time, and whose end is fixed (mabnī) on the fatḥa, whether its letters are few or many, except by an accident”. Fixed means that its end does not change with a governor; the “accident” (ʿāriḍ) is what is joined to it, as the tables will show: faʿalū before the wāw of the group, faʿaltu before a vowelled pronoun.

It has four patterns: faʿala, faʿila, faʿula and faʿlala, as ḍaraba, “he hit”, samiʿa, “he heard”, karuma, “he was noble”, and baʿthara, “he scattered”. The first three have three radicals and differ only in the vowel of the middle one; the fourth has four.

The letters f, ʿ and l are the scale (mīzān) of the title: every verb is weighed on them. In ḍaraba the ḍ stands in the place of the f, and is called the fāʾ of the word; the r is its ʿayn; the b is its lām. A fourth radical is matched by a second lām, as in baʿthara, faʿlala. The student who can weigh a word can find its pattern, and from the pattern all its forms.

tasks.prompt: Weigh ḍaraba, samiʿa and karuma on the scale, and name the fāʾ, ʿayn and lām of ḍaraba.

tasks.prompt: What are the three times of the verb, and what “branches off” from them?
tasks.answer: Past, future and present. Every other form, the imperative, the prohibition, the participles and the rest, is built from them.

tasks.prompt: Why is baʿthara weighed faʿlala, with two lāms?
tasks.answer: It has four radicals, b-ʿ-th-r. The scale has only three letters, so the fourth radical is matched by repeating the lām: faʿlala.

text.original: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، وَالْعَاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ، وَالصَّلَاةُ عَلَى رَسُولِهِ مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ وَأَصْحَابِهِ أَجْمَعِينَ.
text.en: Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds; the [good] end is for the godfearing; and blessing be upon His messenger Muḥammad, and upon his family and his Companions, all of them.

text.original: بدان أَسْعَدَكَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى فِي الدَّارَيْنِ که جملهٔ افعال منصرفه بر سه گونه است: ماضی و مستقبل و حال، و هر چه جز این سه چیز است متفرع است هم ازین سه.
text.en: Know — may God Most High make you happy in both abodes — that all the conjugated verbs are of three kinds: past (māḍī), future (mustaqbal) and present (ḥāl); and whatever is other than these three things branches off from these three.

text.original: اما ماضی فعلی را گویند که بزمانه گذشته تعلق دارد و آخر او مبنی باشد بر فتحه، قَلَّتْ حُرُوفُهُ أَوْ كَثُرَتْ، مگر بعارض، چون فَعَلَ فَعِلَ فَعُلَ فَعْلَلَ، چون ضَرَبَ سَمِعَ كَرُمَ بَعْثَرَ.
text.en: The past is the name of a verb that relates to past time and whose end is fixed (mabnī) on the fatḥa, whether its letters are few or many, except by an accident (ʿāriḍ); as faʿala, faʿila, faʿula and faʿlala, as ḍaraba “he hit”, samiʿa “he heard”, karuma “he was noble” and baʿthara “he scattered”.

lessons.title: The future and the present; the fourteen forms
body: The future (mustaqbal) is “a verb that relates to time to come, and whose end is marfūʿ, except by an accident”, a governor such as lan or lam, which the later tables bring. Its patterns follow those of the past: yafʿalu, yafʿilu, yafʿulu and yufaʿlilu, as yaḍribu, yasmaʿu, yakrumu and yubaʿthiru. The present (ḥāl) “relates to the time that now is”, and its form is the same as the future's: yaḍribu is “he hits” or “he will hit”, and only the context tells which. That is why the book speaks of one form, which other books call the muḍāriʿ.

“From each of these, the past and the muḍāriʿ, fourteen words come out”: three for the masculine absent, three for the feminine absent, three for the masculine present, three for the feminine present, and two for “the speaker's report of himself” (ḥikāyat nafs al-mutakallim). Each three is one, two and many. The madrasas of India name the persons with these words: ghāʾib, “absent”, for the third person; ḥāḍir, “present”, for the one addressed; mutakallim for the speaker.
In the two forms of the speaker, masculine and feminine are the same: faʿaltu, “I did”, is said by a man or a woman; and faʿalnā, “we did”, by two or many, men or women. So 6 + 6 + 2 = 14.

Each of past and muḍāriʿ is active (maʿrūf), its doer known, or passive (majhūl), its doer not named; and each of these is affirmative (ithbāt) or negative (nafy). The book follows this order table by table: active, passive, negated active, negated passive. The student learns each table by heart and can name every form in it: faʿalat is “the singular feminine absent of the affirmative active past”.

text.original: اما مستقبل فعلی را گویند که بزمانه آینده تعلق دارد و آخر او مرفوع باشد مگر بعارض، چون يَفْعَلُ يَفْعِلُ يَفْعُلُ يُفَعْلِلُ، چون يَضْرِبُ يَسْمَعُ يَكْرُمُ يُبَعْثِرُ. اما حال فعلی را گویند که بزمانه موجود تعلق دارد، و صیغه حال همچو صیغه استقبال است.
text.en: The future is the name of a verb that relates to time to come and whose end is marfūʿ, except by an accident; as yafʿalu, yafʿilu, yafʿulu and yufaʿlilu, as yaḍribu “he hits”, yasmaʿu “he hears”, yakrumu “he is noble” and yubaʿthiru “he scatters”. The present is the name of a verb that relates to the time that now is, and the form of the present is like the form of the future.

text.original: و از هر یکی ازین ماضی و مضارع چهارده کلمه بیرون می آید: سه ازان مر مذکر غائب راست، و سه ازان مر مؤنث غائبه راست، و سه ازان مر مذکر حاضر راست، و سه ازان مر مؤنث حاضره راست، و دو ازان مر حکایت نفس متکلم راست.
text.en: From each of these, the past and the muḍāriʿ, fourteen words come out: three of them are for the masculine absent, three for the feminine absent, three for the masculine present [the one addressed], three for the feminine present, and two for the speaker's report of himself (ḥikāyat nafs al-mutakallim).

text.original: و در اول صیغه وحدان حکایت نفس متکلم مذکر و مؤنث یکسان است، و در دوم صیغه حکایت نفس متکلم تثنیه و جمع مذکر و مؤنث نیز یکسان است. و هر یکی ازین ماضی و مضارع بر دو گونه است: معروف و مجهول، و هر یکی ازین نیز بر دو گونه است: اثبات و نفی.
text.en: In the first, the singular form of the speaker's report of himself, masculine and feminine are the same; and in the second, the form of the speaker's report of himself for the dual and the plural, masculine and feminine are also the same. Each of these, the past and the muḍāriʿ, is of two kinds: active (maʿrūf) and passive (majhūl); and each of these is again of two kinds: affirmative (ithbāt) and negative (nafy).

lessons.title: The affirmative active past
body: The first table is faʿala in its fourteen forms. Read it in threes: faʿala, faʿalā, faʿalū, “he did, they two did, they did”; faʿalat, faʿalatā, faʿalna, for women; faʿalta, faʿaltumā, faʿaltum, to men addressed; faʿalti, faʿaltumā, faʿaltunna, to women addressed; and faʿaltu, faʿalnā, the speaker.

The stem faʿal- does not change; what changes is the ending. Some endings are pronouns, the doer itself: the alif of the dual (-ā), the wāw of the group (-ū), the nūn of the women (-na), and the tāʾ of the one addressed or of the speaker (-ta, -tumā, -tum, -ti, -tunna, -tu), and -nā. One is only a sign: the tāʾ of the feminine in faʿalat, which marks a feminine doer but is not the doer.

Here is the “accident” of the first lesson. The end, the lām, keeps its fatḥa in faʿala, faʿalā, faʿalat and faʿalatā. Before the wāw of the group it takes a ḍamma, faʿalū; before the vowelled pronouns it takes a sukūn: faʿalna, faʿalta, faʿaltu, faʿalnā.

Two forms are alike: faʿaltumā is both “you two men did” and “you two women did”, and the book writes it twice to keep the fourteen. Once the table is learnt, every sound verb of the pattern goes the same way: naṣara, naṣarā, naṣarū, “he helped, they two helped, they helped”.

lessons.title: The passive past
body: “When you want to build the passive, give the fāʾ of the verb a ḍamma and the ʿayn of the verb a kasra in all fourteen, and leave the lām of the word as it is.” Faʿala becomes fuʿila, “it was done”; faʿalū becomes fuʿilū, “they were done”; faʿaltu becomes fuʿiltu, “I was done”.

The rule touches only the first two radicals. The endings of the active table stay as they were, and so do the vowels of the lām: fuʿilū with ḍamma, fuʿilna with sukūn. So one who knows the active table knows the passive one: change two vowels and read on.

The passive does not name the doer. In naṣara Zaydun ʿAmran, “Zayd helped ʿAmr”, the doer is Zayd; in nuṣira ʿAmrun, “ʿAmr was helped”, the one helped stands in his place. The same rule gives nuṣira from naṣara and ḍuriba from ḍaraba, whatever the vowel of the active ʿayn.

The book says “in all fourteen” on purpose: the beginner is tempted to change only the first form and copy the rest from the active. Every form of the passive past has u … i at its start: fuʿiltunna, fuʿilnā.

lessons.title: The negated past with mā
body: To negate the past, “bring in the mā of negation at its beginning”: mā faʿala, “he did not do”; mā fuʿila, “it was not done”. The rule is the same for the active and the passive, and for all fourteen forms.

“The mā of negation has no effect at all on the wording of the past”: faʿala stays faʿala, faʿalū stays faʿalū. “But it has an effect on the meaning: it turns the affirmative into the meaning of the negative.” The book draws the student's eye to this distinction because the next particles, lan and lam, will change the wording too.

So the two tables of this lesson are the two tables of the last lessons, each word with mā before it: mā faʿala, mā faʿalā, mā faʿalū … mā faʿalnā; mā fuʿila … mā fuʿilnā. With naṣara: mā naṣara, “he did not help”; mā nuṣira, “he was not helped”.

Do not confuse this mā with the other mās of Arabic. Before a past verb in these tables it only negates; the mā of mā aḥsana, “how fine!”, or the mā of “what”, are other words, which the books of naḥw teach.

tasks.prompt: What does the book mean by saying that mā has no effect on the wording but an effect on the meaning?
tasks.answer: The form of the verb stays exactly as it was (faʿala, faʿalū…), but the sentence now denies what it affirmed: “he did” becomes “he did not do”.

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث اثبات فعل ماضی مجهول بود. چون خواهی که نفی بنا کنی، مای نفی در اول او در آر تا ماضی منفی گردد، و مای نفی در لفظ ماضی هیچ عمل نکند، چنانچه بود همبران طریق باشد، لیکن عمل در معنی کند، یعنی مثبت را بمعنی منفی گرداند.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the affirmative passive past verb. When you want to build the negative, bring in the mā of negation at its beginning, so that it becomes the negated past. The mā of negation has no effect at all on the wording of the past — it stays as it was —, but it has an effect on the meaning, that is, it turns the affirmative into the meaning of the negative.

lessons.title: Useful notes: the near, far, continuous, supposed and wished past
body: Our print adds a box of “useful notes” (fawāʾid nāfiʿa) inside the text; it is not in every copy of the Mīzān. What has been taught so far is the absolute past (māḍī muṭlaq): faʿala, “he did”. With a word put before it, the past takes finer shades of time and mood.

Qad before it makes the near past (qarīb): qad ḍaraba, “he has hit”, just now. Kāna before it makes the far past (baʿīd): kāna ḍaraba, “he had hit”. Kāna before the muḍāriʿ makes the continuous past (istimrārī): kāna yafʿalu, “he used to do”, “he was doing”.

Laʿallamā before the past makes the past of supposition (iḥtimālī): laʿallamā faʿala, “perhaps he did”. Laytamā makes the past of wishing (tamannāʾī): laytamā ḍaraba, “would that he had hit”. “From each of these come fourteen forms”, as from the absolute past.

The six names are those of the Persian pasts that the student already knows from his own language, the māżī-yi muṭlaq, qarīb, baʿīd, istimrārī, iḥtimālī and tamannāʾī. The box uses them to show how each Persian tense is said in Arabic, which is why it fits a Persian primer.

text.original: این همه که گفته شد بحث ماضی مطلق بود. چون خواهی که ماضی قریب یا بعید یا استمراری وغیره بنا کنی، پس اگر لفظ قَدْ بر ماضی مطلق داخل کنی ماضی قریب گردد، چون قَدْ ضَرَبَ، و اگر لفظ كَانَ داخل کنی ماضی بعید شود، نحو: كَانَ ضَرَبَ،
text.en: All that has been said was on the absolute past (māḍī muṭlaq). When you want to build the near past (qarīb), the far past (baʿīd), the continuous past (istimrārī) and the like: if you put the word qad before the absolute past, it becomes the near past, as qad ḍaraba “he has hit”; and if you put the word kāna before it, it becomes the far past, as kāna ḍaraba “he had hit”;

text.original: و اگر آن را بر مضارع داخل کنی ماضی استمراری گردد، چون كَانَ يَفْعَلُ، و اگر بر ماضی مطلق لفظ لَعَلَّمَا در آری ماضی احتمالی گردد، نحو: لَعَلَّمَا فَعَلَ، و همچنان اگر بجای لَعَلَّمَا لفظ لَيْتَمَا داخل کنی ماضی تمنائی گردد، چون لَيْتَمَا ضَرَبَ. باید دانست که از هر یک اینها چهارده چهارده صیغه بر می آید، چنانکه در ماضی مطلق گذشت.
text.en: and if you put it before the muḍāriʿ, it becomes the continuous past, as kāna yafʿalu “he used to do”; and if you bring the word laʿallamā before the absolute past, it becomes the past of supposition (iḥtimālī), as laʿallamā faʿala “perhaps he did”; and likewise, if in place of laʿallamā you put the word laytamā, it becomes the past of wishing (tamannāʾī), as laytamā ḍaraba “would that he had hit”. It should be known that from each of these come fourteen forms, as has passed in the absolute past.

lessons.title: Building the muḍāriʿ: the signs atayna and the nūn of iʿrāb
body: “When you want to build the muḍāriʿ, bring in one of the signs of the muḍāriʿ at its beginning and give its end a ḍamma.” The signs are four letters, alif, tāʾ, yāʾ and nūn, which together spell atayna, “they (women) came”, a word to remember them by. Faʿala becomes yafʿulu; Mīzān's paradigm has a ḍamma on the ʿayn, the pattern of naṣara yanṣuru.

Each sign has its forms. The alif is for the speaker alone: afʿulu, “I do”. The nūn is for the speaker with others: nafʿulu, “we do”. The yāʾ is for four forms: the three of the masculine absent and the plural of the feminine absent, yafʿulna. The tāʾ is for the other eight: the six of the present, and the singular and dual of the feminine absent, tafʿulu, “she does”, tafʿulāni.

“In seven places bring in the nūn of iʿrāb”: the four duals, with a kasra (-āni), and the two masculine plurals and the singular feminine present, with a fatḥa (-ūna, -īna). This nūn is the sign of rafʿ, and it will drop under lan and lam. The nūn of the feminine plural, yafʿulna, tafʿulna, is another nūn: it comes in the muḍāriʿ as in the past (faʿalna), it is the doer itself, and it stays.

Read the table with this in mind. Tafʿulu is written twice, for “she” and for “you (m.)”; tafʿulāni three times, for the two women absent and for the two men and two women addressed. The context tells them apart. With naṣara: yanṣuru, yanṣurāni, yanṣurūna.

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث فعل ماضی بود. چون خواهی که مضارع بنا کنی، یکی را از علامتهای مضارع در اول او در آر و آخر او را ضمه کن، و علامات مضارع چهار حرف اند: الف و تا و یا و نون، که مجموع وی أَتَيْنَ باشد.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the past verb. When you want to build the muḍāriʿ, bring in one of the signs of the muḍāriʿ at its beginning and give its end a ḍamma. The signs of the muḍāriʿ are four letters, alif, tāʾ, yāʾ and nūn, which together make atayna.

text.original: الف وحدان حکایت نفس متکلم راست، و تا برای هشت کلمه است: سه ازان مر مذکر حاضر راست، و سه ازان مر مؤنث حاضره راست، و دو ازان مر واحد و تثنیه مؤنث غائبه است، و یا برای چهار کلمه است: سه ازان مر مذکر غائب راست، و یکی مر جمع مؤنث غائبه راست، و نون برای تثنیه و جمع حکایت نفس متکلم مذکر و مؤنث است.
text.en: The alif is for the singular of the speaker's report of himself. The tāʾ is for eight words: three of them for the masculine present, three for the feminine present, and two for the singular and the dual of the feminine absent. The yāʾ is for four words: three of them for the masculine absent and one for the plural of the feminine absent. And the nūn is for the dual and the plural of the speaker's report of himself, masculine and feminine.

text.original: و در هفت محل نون اعرابی را در آر: چهار تثنیه، که نون اعرابی در اینها مکسور باشد، و دو جمع مذکر غائب و حاضر، و یکی واحد مؤنث حاضره، که نون اعرابی در اینها مفتوح باشد، و نون جمع مؤنث چنانکه در ماضی آید همچنان در مضارع نیز آید.
text.en: In seven places bring in the nūn of iʿrāb: the four duals, in which the nūn of iʿrāb has a kasra; and the two plurals of the masculine absent and present, and the one singular of the feminine present, in which the nūn of iʿrāb has a fatḥa. The nūn of the feminine plural comes in the muḍāriʿ too, just as it comes in the past.

lessons.title: The passive muḍāriʿ
body: “When you want to build the passive muḍāriʿ, give the sign of the muḍāriʿ a ḍamma and the ʿayn of the word a fatḥa in all fourteen, and leave the lām as it is.” Yafʿulu becomes yufʿalu, “it is done”; tafʿulūna becomes tufʿalūna; afʿulu becomes ufʿalu.

Compare the passive past: there the fāʾ took a ḍamma and the ʿayn a kasra (fuʿila); here the sign takes the ḍamma and the ʿayn a fatḥa (yufʿalu). The fāʾ of the muḍāriʿ is already quiescent and stays so. Two vowels again, but other ones: u … i in the past, u … a in the muḍāriʿ.

The ʿayn of the passive muḍāriʿ is a fatḥa whatever it was in the active: yanṣuru becomes yunṣaru, yaḍribu becomes yuḍrabu, yasmaʿu becomes yusmaʿu. The endings, the nūn of iʿrāb and the nūn of the women all stay as in the active table.

So the beginner who knows yafʿulu knows yufʿalu: tafʿulīna → tufʿalīna, yafʿulna → yufʿalna. A common slip is to keep the fatḥa of the sign (yafʿalu): then the word is an active verb of another pattern, not a passive.

lessons.title: Negating the muḍāriʿ with lā
body: To negate the muḍāriʿ, “bring in the lā of negation at its beginning”: lā yafʿulu, “he does not do”, or “he will not do”; lā yufʿalu, “it is not done”.

Lā is to the muḍāriʿ what mā was to the past: “it has no effect at all on the wording of the muḍāriʿ”. The end keeps its ḍamma, the nūn of iʿrāb stays: lā yafʿulāni, lā yafʿulūna, lā tafʿulīna. “But it has an effect on the meaning”: the affirmative becomes negative.
The two tables are the two tables of the muḍāriʿ with lā before each word: active lā yafʿulu … lā nafʿulu; passive lā yufʿalu … lā nufʿalu. With naṣara: lā yanṣuru, “he does not help”.

Mark this lā well, because the book will bring another lā later, the lā of prohibition, which does change the wording: lā tafʿul, “do not do!”. Lā tafʿulu, with its ḍamma, only negates; lā tafʿul, with a sukūn, forbids.

text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the affirmative passive muḍāriʿ verb. When you want to build the negative, bring in the lā of negation at its beginning. The lā of negation has no effect at all on the wording of the muḍāriʿ — it stays as it was —, but it has an effect on the meaning, that is, it turns the affirmative into the meaning of the negative.

lessons.title: The emphatic negation with lan
body: “Bring in lan at the beginning of the muḍāriʿ; this negation is called the emphatic negation with lan (nafy-i taʾkīd ba-lan).” Lan yafʿula, “he will not do”, “he will never do”. Unlike mā and lā, lan changes the wording, and the book says exactly where.

“Lan puts the future in naṣb in five places”: the singular masculine absent, the singular feminine absent, the singular masculine present, and the two forms of the speaker. These are the five forms that end in a ḍamma: yafʿulu → lan yafʿula, tafʿulu → lan tafʿula, afʿulu → lan afʿula, nafʿulu → lan nafʿula.

“And in seven places it makes the nūn of iʿrāb drop”: the four duals, the two masculine plurals and the singular feminine present: lan yafʿulā, lan yafʿulū, lan tafʿulī. “And in two words, the plurals of the feminine absent and present, it has no effect in the wording”: lan yafʿulna, lan tafʿulna, since their nūn is the pronoun of the women, not a sign of rafʿ. 5 + 7 + 2 = 14.

In meaning, “lan turns the muḍāriʿ into the meaning of a negated future”: the present sense of yafʿulu is gone, and only “will not” is left. The passive table follows the same three rules: lan yufʿala, lan yufʿalā, lan yufʿalna.

lessons.title: The negation of denial with lam
body: “Bring in lam at the beginning of the muḍāriʿ; this negation is called the negation of denial with lam (nafy-i jaḥd ba-lam).” Lam yafʿul, “he did not do”. Like lan, lam changes the wording, in the same places, but in another way.

“Lam puts the muḍāriʿ in jazm in five places, if there is no weak letter at its end”: the same five as with lan, he, she, you (m.), I and we, but with a sukūn where lan gave a fatḥa: lam yafʿul, lam tafʿul, lam afʿul, lam nafʿul. “And if there is one, it makes it drop”: lam yadʿu, “he did not call”, lam yarmi, “he did not throw”, lam yakhsha, “he did not fear”. The weak letters are three, wāw, alif and yāʾ, “which together make āy”.

In the other places lam does what lan did: “in seven places it makes the nūn of iʿrāb drop”, lam yafʿulā, lam yafʿulū, lam tafʿulī; and “in two places it has no effect in the wording”, the two feminine plurals, lam yafʿulna, lam tafʿulna.

In meaning, “it turns the form of the muḍāriʿ into the meaning of a negated past”: lam yafʿul is “he did not do”, the same in sense as mā faʿala. The beginner should hold lan and lam side by side: the same seven and the same two; only the five differ, fatḥa against sukūn, and “will not” against “did not”.

parts.title: The lām and the nūns of emphasis

lessons.title: The lām and the two nūns of emphasis: the rules
body: To make the future emphatic, “bring in the lām of emphasis at the beginning of the future verb and add the nūn of emphasis at its end”: la-yafʿulanna, “he will surely do”. The lām “always has a fatḥa”. The nūn is of two kinds: the heavy nūn (thaqīla), doubled, -nna; and the light nūn (khafīfa), quiescent, -n.

“The heavy nūn comes in fourteen words, the light nūn in eight.” What comes before the heavy nūn depends on the form. In five places a fatḥa: he, she, you (m.), I and we, la-yafʿulanna, la-tafʿulanna, la-afʿulanna, la-nafʿulanna. In six places an alif: the four duals, la-yafʿulānni, and the two feminine plurals, la-yafʿulnānni, where the alif “comes as a separator” (fāṣil) between the nūn of the women and the nūn of emphasis.

In the two masculine plurals the wāw is dropped and the ḍamma before it is kept, “to point to the dropping of the wāw”: la-yafʿulunna, from la-yafʿulūnanna. In the singular feminine present the yāʾ is dropped and the kasra kept, to point to it: la-tafʿulinna. The heavy nūn has a kasra in the six places with the alif (-ānni) and a fatḥa in the other eight (-anna, -unna, -inna).

“The light nūn does not come in a place where there is an alif”: so not in the four duals nor in the two feminine plurals, which leaves eight forms. And “the nūn of iʿrāb does not come together with the nūn of emphasis”: yafʿulūna loses its nūn of rafʿ before the nūn of emphasis, as before lan and lam.

When you want to build the lām of emphasis with the nūn of emphasis, bring in the lām of emphasis at the beginning of the future verb and add the nūn of emphasis at its end. The lām of emphasis always has a fatḥa. The nūn of emphasis is two nūns: one the heavy nūn, the second the light nūn. The heavy nūn is the name of the doubled nūn, and the light nūn is the name of the unvowelled nūn.

text.original: و نون ثقیله در چهارده کلمه در آید، و نون خفیفه در هشت کلمه در آید، و ما قبل نون ثقیله در پنج محل مفتوح باشد، و آن پنج محل اینست: واحد مذکر غائب، و واحد مؤنث غائبه، و واحد مذکر حاضر، و دو صیغه حکایت نفس متکلم،
text.en: The heavy nūn comes in fourteen words, and the light nūn in eight words. The letter before the heavy nūn has a fatḥa in five places, and these five places are: the masculine singular absent, the feminine singular absent, the masculine singular present, and the two forms of the speaker's report of himself;

text.original: و در شش محل ما قبل نون ثقیله الف باشد: چهار تثنیه، و دو جمع مؤنث غائبه و حاضره، و درین دو محل الف فاصل آید، و در جمع مذکر غائب و حاضر واو دور کرده شود و ما قبل او ضمه گذاشته شود تا دلالت کند بر حذف واو، و از صیغه واحد مؤنث حاضره یا دور کرده شود و ما قبل او کسره گذاشته آید تا دلالت کند بر حذف یا.
text.en: in six places there is an alif before the heavy nūn: the four duals, and the two plurals of the feminine absent and present, and in these two places the alif comes as a separator (fāṣil). In the plural of the masculine absent and present the wāw is removed, and the letter before it is left with a ḍamma, to point to the dropping of the wāw; and from the form of the singular feminine present the yāʾ is removed, and the letter before it is left with a kasra, to point to the dropping of the yāʾ.

text.original: و نون ثقیله در شش محل مکسور باشد، و آن شش محل آنست که در آن الف در می آید، و در باقی هشت محل مفتوح، و نون خفیفه در محلی که الف باشد در نیاید، و در باقی محل در آید، و نون اعرابی با نون تأکید جمع نشود.
text.en: The heavy nūn has a kasra in six places, and these six places are those in which the alif comes; in the other eight places it has a fatḥa. The light nūn does not come in a place where there is an alif, and it comes in the other places. The nūn of iʿrāb does not come together with the nūn of emphasis.

lessons.title: The future with the heavy and the light nūn
body: Now the tables. The heavy nūn, active: la-yafʿulanna, la-yafʿulānni, la-yafʿulunna, la-tafʿulanna, la-tafʿulānni, la-yafʿulnānni, and so on to la-afʿulanna, la-nafʿulanna. Every rule of the last lesson can be seen in it: the fatḥa in the five, the alif and the kasra of the nūn in the six, the ḍamma and the kasra that mark the dropped wāw and yāʾ.
The passive goes the same way on yufʿalu: la-yufʿalanna, “it will surely be done”, la-yufʿalānni, la-yufʿalunna, la-tufʿalinna. Only the vowels of the stem change, u … a, as in every passive muḍāriʿ.

The light nūn has eight forms: la-yafʿulan, la-yafʿulun, la-tafʿulan, la-tafʿulan, la-tafʿulun, la-tafʿulin, la-afʿulan, la-nafʿulan. La-tafʿulan comes twice, as the print writes it: once for “she”, once for “you (m.)”. Its meaning is the same as the heavy nūn's, a little less strong.
Learn the two tables together, form by form, with the grid: where the heavy nūn has an alif before it, the light nūn has no form at all.

lessons.title: Building the imperative
body: “The imperative is taken from the muḍāriʿ: the absent from the absent, the present from the present, the speaker from the speaker, the active from the active, the passive from the passive.” There is no separate root for the command; one starts from tafʿulu and changes it.

For the active imperative to the one present, “drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ, then see whether what follows remains vowelled or quiescent”. If it is vowelled, simply make the end quiescent: taʿidu, “you promise”, gives ʿid, “promise!”; taḍaʿu gives ḍaʿ, “put!”; and if the end is a weak letter, it drops: taqī gives qi, “guard!”. These are verbs whose first radical, a wāw, has already gone in the muḍāriʿ.

If what follows the sign is quiescent, a word cannot begin with it, so a hamza of connection is added, and its vowel depends on the ʿayn. If the ʿayn has a kasra or a fatḥa, the hamza takes a kasra: tasmaʿu → ismaʿ, “hear!”; taḍribu → iḍrib, “hit!”; with a weak end, tarmī → irmi, takhshā → ikhsha. If the ʿayn has a ḍamma, the hamza takes a ḍamma: tanṣuru → unṣur, “help!”; tadʿū → udʿu, “call!”.

For the passive imperative to the one present, and for both imperatives to the absent, the lām of command is used, with a kasra, and the end is put in jazm, or a weak letter dropped: li-yadʿu, “let him call”, li-yarmi, li-yakhsha. “The nūn of emphasis comes in the imperative too, as in the muḍāriʿ; and in the imperative the nūn of iʿrāb drops as well.”

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث فعل مستقبل با نون ثقیله و خفیفه بود. چون خواهی که امر بنا کنی، امر گرفته میشود از فعل مضارع: غائب از غائب، حاضر از حاضر، متکلم از متکلم، معروف از معروف، مجهول از مجهول.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the future verb with the heavy and the light nūn. When you want to build the imperative: the imperative is taken from the muḍāriʿ verb, the absent from the absent, the present from the present, the speaker from the speaker, the active from the active and the passive from the passive.

text.original: چون خواهی که امر حاضر معروف بنا کنی، علامت مضارع را حذف کن، بعده بنگر که متحرک میماند یا ساکن؛ اگر متحرک میماند آخر را ساکن کن اگر حرف علت نباشد، چون از تَعِدُ عِدْ و از تَضَعُ ضَعْ، و اگر باشد ساقط شود، چون از تَقِي قِ.
text.en: When you want to build the active imperative to the one present, drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ; then see whether [what follows] remains vowelled or unvowelled. If it remains vowelled, make the end unvowelled if it is not a weak letter, as from taʿidu “you promise” ʿid “promise!” and from taḍaʿu “you put” ḍaʿ “put!”; and if it is, it drops, as from taqī “you guard” qi “guard!”.

text.original: و اگر ساکن میماند نظر کن در عین کلمه؛ اگر عین کلمه مکسور باشد یا مفتوح، همزه وصل مکسور در اول در آر و آخر را ساکن کن اگر حرف علت نباشد، چون از تَسْمَعُ اِسْمَعْ و از تَضْرِبُ اِضْرِبْ، و اگر باشد ساقط شود، چون از تَرْمِي اِرْمِ و از تَخْشَى اِخْشَ؛ و اگر عین کلمه مضموم باشد همزه وصل مضموم در اول او در آر و آخر را ساکن کن اگر حرف علت نباشد، چون از تَنْصُرُ اُنْصُرْ، و اگر باشد ساقط شود، چون از تَدْعُو اُدْعُ.
text.en: If it remains unvowelled, look at the ʿayn of the word. If the ʿayn of the word has a kasra or a fatḥa, bring in a hamza of connection with kasra at the beginning and make the end unvowelled if it is not a weak letter, as from tasmaʿu “you hear” ismaʿ “hear!” and from taḍribu “you hit” iḍrib “hit!”; and if it is, it drops, as from tarmī “you throw” irmi “throw!” and from takhshā “you fear” ikhsha “fear!”. If the ʿayn of the word has a ḍamma, bring in a hamza of connection with ḍamma at its beginning and make the end unvowelled if it is not a weak letter, as from tanṣuru “you help” unṣur “help!”; and if it is, it drops, as from tadʿū “you call” udʿu “call!”.

text.original: چون خواهی که امر حاضر مجهول یا امر غائب معروف یا مجهول بنا کنی، لام امر مکسور در اول او در آر و آخر او را جزم کن اگر حرف علت نباشد، و اگر باشد ساقط شود، چون لِيَدْعُ لِيَرْمِ لِيَخْشَ. و نون تأکید چنانچه در مضارع می آید در امر نیز می آید، و در امر نون اعرابی هم ساقط شود.
text.en: When you want to build the passive imperative to the one present, or the active or passive imperative to the absent, bring in the lām of command with kasra at its beginning and put its end in jazm if it is not a weak letter; and if it is, it drops, as li-yadʿu “let him call”, li-yarmi “let him throw” and li-yakhsha “let him fear”. The nūn of emphasis comes in the imperative too, just as it comes in the muḍāriʿ; and in the imperative the nūn of iʿrāb drops as well.

lessons.title: The imperative to the present and to the absent
body: The active imperative to the one present has six forms: ufʿul, ufʿulā, ufʿulū, ufʿulī, ufʿulā, ufʿulna, “do!” to one man, two, many, one woman, two, many. The hamza has a ḍamma because the ʿayn of yafʿulu has one; each form is the muḍāriʿ in jazm without its sign, tafʿulū → ufʿulū.

The passive imperative to the one present takes the lām instead: li-tufʿal, li-tufʿalā, li-tufʿalū, li-tufʿalī, li-tufʿalā, li-tufʿalna, “be done!”. A hamza could not do here what it does in the active, because the passive needs its sign, with its ḍamma, to be seen.

The imperative to the absent, active and passive, has eight forms, the six of the absent and two of the speaker: li-yafʿul, li-yafʿulā, li-yafʿulū, li-tafʿul, li-tafʿulā, li-yafʿulna, li-afʿul, li-nafʿul, “let him do … let me do, let us do”; and the passive li-yufʿal … li-nufʿal. So 6 + 8 = 14, as in every table.
The end of every form is as after lam: a sukūn, or the nūn of iʿrāb dropped, or, in the feminine plural, no change. A command is a demand, and the demand puts the verb in jazm.

lessons.title: The imperative with the heavy and the light nūn
body: The nūn of emphasis comes in the imperative as in the muḍāriʿ, with the same rules. With the heavy nūn, to the one present: ufʿulanna, ufʿulānni, ufʿulunna, ufʿulinna, ufʿulānni, ufʿulnānni, “do, surely!”. To the absent: li-yafʿulanna, li-yafʿulānni, li-yafʿulunna, li-tafʿulanna, li-tafʿulānni, li-yafʿulnānni, li-afʿulanna, li-nafʿulanna. The passive goes on li-tufʿalanna and li-yufʿalanna.

Before the heavy nūn: a fatḥa in the singulars (ufʿulanna), an alif in the duals and the feminine plurals with the nūn in kasra (ufʿulānni, ufʿulnānni), the ḍamma of the dropped wāw (ufʿulunna) and the kasra of the dropped yāʾ (ufʿulinna). The sukūn of the imperative gives way to these vowels, since a quiescent letter cannot stand before the doubled nūn.

With the light nūn there are fewer forms, since it never follows an alif: to the one present three, ufʿulan, ufʿulun, ufʿulin; to the absent five, li-yafʿulan, li-yafʿulun, li-tafʿulan, li-afʿulan, li-nafʿulan. The passive has the same three and five: li-tufʿalan, li-tufʿalun, li-tufʿalin; li-yufʿalan … li-nufʿalan.
Eight short tables, but one rule: take the imperative, open its end, and add the nūn as in the emphatic future. The grid sets the active forms side by side.

lessons.title: The prohibition
body: “Bring in the lā of prohibition at the beginning of the future verb.” Lā tafʿul, “do not do!”. The lā of prohibition “puts its end in jazm in five places, like lam”: he, she, you (m.), I and we. If the end is a weak letter, it drops: lā tadʿu, “do not call!”, lā tarmi, “do not throw!”, lā takhsha, “do not fear!”.

Like lam it also “removes the nūn of iʿrāb from seven places”, lā tafʿulā, lā tafʿulū, lā tafʿulī; and “in two places it has no effect on the wording”, lā tafʿulna, lā yafʿulna. The ends of the prohibition are the ends of the imperative; only the lā and the sign of the muḍāriʿ stand before them.

The tables: to the one present, active, lā tafʿul, lā tafʿulā, lā tafʿulū, lā tafʿulī, lā tafʿulā, lā tafʿulna; passive, lā tufʿal …; to the absent and the speaker, lā yafʿul, lā yafʿulā, lā yafʿulū, lā tafʿul, lā tafʿulā, lā yafʿulna, lā afʿul, lā nafʿul, and the passive lā yufʿal … lā nufʿal.

Set this beside lesson 9. Lā tafʿulu, with a ḍamma, is the lā of negation: “you do not do”. Lā tafʿul, with a sukūn, is the lā of prohibition: “do not do!”. The same two letters, lā, are two different words, and the end of the verb tells which.

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث امر بود. چون خواهی که نهی بنا کنی، پس لای نهی در اول فعل مستقبل در آر، و لای نهی در آخر او در پنج محل جزم کند، مثل لم، اگر در آخر او حرف علت نباشد، و اگر باشد ساقط گرداند، چون لَا تَدْعُ وَلَا تَرْمِ وَلَا تَخْشَ، و از هفت محل نون اعرابی را هم دور نماید، و در دو محل در لفظ عمل نکند، و نون تأکید چنانچه در مضارع می آید همبران طریق در نهی نیز می آید.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the imperative. When you want to build the prohibition, bring in the lā of prohibition at the beginning of the future verb. The lā of prohibition puts its end in jazm in five places, like lam, if there is no weak letter at its end, and if there is, it drops it, as lā tadʿu “do not call”, lā tarmi “do not throw” and lā takhsha “do not fear”. It also removes the nūn of iʿrāb from seven places, and in two places it has no effect on the wording. The nūn of emphasis comes in the prohibition in the same way as it comes in the muḍāriʿ.

lessons.title: The prohibition with the heavy and the light nūn
body: “The nūn of emphasis comes in the prohibition in the same way as it comes in the muḍāriʿ.” With the heavy nūn, to the one present: lā tafʿulanna, lā tafʿulānni, lā tafʿulunna, lā tafʿulinna, lā tafʿulānni, lā tafʿulnānni, “do not ever do!”. The passive tables put the stem on yufʿalu: lā tufʿalanna … lā tufʿalnānni; lā yufʿalanna … lā nufʿalanna. Everything before the nūn follows the rules of lesson 12.

With the light nūn, three forms to the one present, lā tafʿulan, lā tafʿulun, lā tafʿulin, and five to the absent, lā yafʿulan, lā yafʿulun, lā tafʿulan, lā afʿulan, lā nafʿulan, with the passive alike. With this the conjugation of the verb is complete: every form of the book's fourteen, in every mood, has now been built from faʿala by rule.
In the madrasa these tables are recited in order, active then passive, heavy then light, until the student can produce any form of any sound verb without the book. The grid shows the active forms.

lessons.title: The active and the passive participle
body: “The active participle is taken from the active muḍāriʿ.” Drop the sign, give the fāʾ a fatḥa, bring in “the alif of fāʿil” between the fāʾ and the ʿayn, give the ʿayn a kasra and add tanwīn: yafʿulu → fāʿilun, “one who does”. With naṣara: nāṣirun, “a helper”, from yanṣuru.
It has six forms, for the noun is declined by gender and number, not by person: fāʿilun, fāʿilāni, fāʿilūna for men; fāʿilatun, fāʿilatāni, fāʿilātun for women.

“The passive participle is made from the passive muḍāriʿ.” Drop the sign, bring in “the mīm of mafʿūl” with a fatḥa at the beginning, give the ʿayn a ḍamma, bring in “the wāw of mafʿūl” between the ʿayn and the lām, and give the lām tanwīn: yufʿalu → mafʿūlun, “one done to”; with naṣara, manṣūrun, “helped”. Its six forms: mafʿūlun, mafʿūlāni, mafʿūlūna, mafʿūlatun, mafʿūlatāni, mafʿūlātun.

These rules are for the bare triliteral. The book builds each noun from the muḍāriʿ, step by step, so that the student sees where every letter comes from: the alif of fāʿil and the mīm and wāw of mafʿūl are added letters, the f, ʿ and l are the root.

tasks.prompt: Build the active participle from yanṣuru, step by step.
tasks.answer: Drop the sign: nṣuru. Give the fāʾ a fatḥa and add the alif: nāṣ-. Give the ʿayn a kasra: nāṣir-. Add tanwīn: nāṣirun.

tasks.prompt: Build the passive participle from yunṣaru, step by step.
tasks.answer: Drop the sign: nṣaru. Add the mīm with fatḥa: manṣ-. Give the ʿayn a ḍamma and add the wāw after it: manṣūr-. Add tanwīn: manṣūrun.

tasks.prompt: Why has the participle six forms, not fourteen?
tasks.answer: It is a noun: it changes for gender and number (one, two, many; masculine, feminine), but not for person, as the verb does.

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث نهی بود. چون خواهی که اسم فاعل بنا کنی، اسم فاعل گرفته میشود از فعل مضارع معروف، پس علامت مضارع را حذف کن، بعد ازان فا کلمه را فتحه ده، و میان فا و عین الف فاعل در آر، و عین کلمه را کسره ده، و لام کلمه را تنوین زیاده کن تا اسم فاعل گردد.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the prohibition. When you want to build the active participle: the active participle is taken from the active muḍāriʿ verb. Drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ; after that give the fāʾ of the word a fatḥa, bring in the alif of fāʿil between the fāʾ and the ʿayn, give the ʿayn of the word a kasra, and add tanwīn to the lām of the word, so that it becomes the active participle.

text.original: فَاعِلٌ، فَاعِلَانِ، فَاعِلُونَ، فَاعِلَةٌ، فَاعِلَتَانِ، فَاعِلَاتٌ
text.en: fāʿilun “one who does (m.)”, fāʿilāni “two who do (m.)”, fāʿilūna “those who do (m.)”, fāʿilatun “one who does (f.)”, fāʿilatāni “two who do (f.)”, fāʿilātun “those who do (f.)”

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث اسم فاعل بود. چون خواهی که اسم مفعول بنا کنی، اسم مفعول ساخته میشود از فعل مضارع مجهول، پس علامت مضارع را حذف کن، بعد ازان میم مفتوح مفعول در اول او در آر، و عین کلمه را ضمه ده، و میان عین و لام واو مفعول در آر، و لام کلمه را تنوین ده تا اسم مفعول گردد.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the active participle. When you want to build the passive participle: the passive participle is made from the passive muḍāriʿ verb. Drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ; after that bring in the mīm of mafʿūl, with fatḥa, at its beginning, give the ʿayn of the word a ḍamma, bring in the wāw of mafʿūl between the ʿayn and the lām, and give the lām of the word tanwīn, so that it becomes the passive participle.

text.original: مَفْعُولٌ، مَفْعُولَانِ، مَفْعُولُونَ، مَفْعُولَةٌ، مَفْعُولَتَانِ، مَفْعُولَاتٌ
text.en: mafʿūlun “a thing done (m.)”, mafʿūlāni “two things done (m.)”, mafʿūlūna “things done (m.)”, mafʿūlatun “a thing done (f.)”, mafʿūlatāni “two things done (f.)”, mafʿūlātun “things done (f.)”

lessons.title: The noun of time and place, and the noun of instrument
body: Our print ends with a supplement (tatimma) on three more nouns, set inside the frame of the text; the transcriber notes that it is a later addition found in Indian prints. Each is again built from the muḍāriʿ.

The noun of time and place (ism ẓarf), the time or place of the act: drop the sign, put a mīm with a fatḥa at the beginning, “give the ʿayn a fatḥa if it has a ḍamma, otherwise leave it as it is”, and add tanwīn. From yafʿulu, with its ḍamma, comes mafʿalun; from a muḍāriʿ with a kasra the kasra would stay. Its forms: mafʿalun, mafʿalāni, and the broken plural mafāʿilu.

The noun of instrument (ism āla), the tool with which the act is done: drop the sign, put a mīm with a kasra, give the ʿayn a fatḥa, add tanwīn: mifʿalun. “If you bring in an alif after the ʿayn, or add a tāʾ after the lām, two other forms appear”: mifʿālun and mifʿalatun. Their forms: mifʿalun, mifʿalatun, mifʿalāni, mifʿalatāni, with the plural mafāʿilu; and mifʿālun, mifʿālāni, with the plural mafāʿīlu.

The book says these forms “mostly agree with the rule”: many nouns of place and instrument in use follow other patterns, which the larger books of ṣarf list. Here the student learns the rule on faʿala; the vowel of the mīm is the first thing to see: ma- for a place, mi- for a tool.

tasks.prompt: How do the noun of place and the noun of instrument differ in their first vowel?
tasks.answer: The noun of time and place has a mīm with fatḥa (mafʿal); the noun of instrument a mīm with kasra (mifʿal).

tasks.prompt: Why is the ʿayn of mafʿal a fatḥa in the book's paradigm?
tasks.answer: The rule is to give the ʿayn a fatḥa if it has a ḍamma in the muḍāriʿ, and to leave it otherwise. Yafʿulu has a ḍamma, so it becomes mafʿal.

tasks.prompt: Give the two other forms of the noun of instrument, and their plurals.
tasks.answer: Mifʿālun, with an alif after the ʿayn, plural mafāʿīlu; and mifʿalatun, with a tāʾ after the lām, plural mafāʿilu.

text.original: فصل: چون خواهی که اسم ظرف زمان و مکان بنا کنی، علامت مضارع را حذف کن و میم مفتوح در اول او در آر، و عین کلمه را فتحه ده اگر مضموم باشد، ورنه بحالش بگذار، و لام کلمه را تنوین ملحق کن تا اسم زمان و مکان گردد.
text.en: Section. When you want to build the noun of time and place (ism ẓarf), drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ and bring in a mīm with fatḥa at its beginning; give the ʿayn of the word a fatḥa if it has a ḍamma, otherwise leave it as it is; and join tanwīn to the lām of the word, so that it becomes the noun of time and place.

text.original: مَفْعَلٌ، مَفْعَلَانِ، مَفَاعِلُ
text.en: mafʿalun “a time or place of doing”, mafʿalāni “two times or places of doing”, mafāʿilu “times or places of doing”

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث اسم ظرف بود. چون خواهی که اسم آله بنا کنی، علامت مضارع را حذف کن و میم مکسور در اول او در آر، و عین کلمه را فتحه ده اگر مفتوح نباشد، و لام کلمه را تنوین ملحق ساز تا اسم آله گردد، و اگر بعد عین کلمه الف آری و یا پس لام تا زیاده کنی، دو صیغه دیگر اسم آله که اکثر موافق قیاس است پدید می آید.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the noun of time and place. When you want to build the noun of instrument, drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ and bring in a mīm with kasra at its beginning; give the ʿayn of the word a fatḥa if it has none, and join tanwīn to the lām of the word, so that it becomes the noun of instrument. If you bring in an alif after the ʿayn of the word, or add a tāʾ after the lām, two other forms of the noun of instrument appear, which mostly agree with the rule.

مِفْعَلٌ، مِفْعَلَةٌ، مِفْعَلَانِ، مِفْعَلَتَانِ
مَفَاعِلُ، وَمِفْعَالٌ، مِفْعَالَانِ، مَفَاعِيلُ
text.en:
mifʿalun “an instrument of doing”, mifʿalatun “an instrument of doing”, mifʿalāni “two instruments of doing”, mifʿalatāni “two instruments of doing”
mafāʿilu “instruments of doing”, wa-mifʿālun “an instrument of doing”, mifʿālāni “two instruments of doing”, mafāʿīlu “instruments of doing”

lessons.title: The elative
body: The elative (ism al-tafḍīl) says that one has more of a quality than another. For the masculine, “drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ, bring in the hamza of the elative at its beginning, give the ʿayn a fatḥa if it has none, and do not join tanwīn to the lām”: yafʿulu → afʿalu, “more doing”.

No tanwīn, because afʿal is a diptote: it has the pattern of a verb (afʿalu, like the muḍāriʿ of the speaker) and is an adjective. The masculine forms: afʿalu, afʿalāni, afʿalūna, and the broken plural afāʿilu.

For the feminine, “after dropping the sign, give the fāʾ a ḍamma, make the ʿayn quiescent, join the short alif (alif maqṣūra) after the lām, and give the lām a fatḥa”: fuʿlā. Its forms: fuʿlā, fuʿlayāni, fuʿlayātun, and the broken plural fuʿalun. The pair is familiar: akbar, “greater”, and kubrā, “greatest (f.)”, as in Allāhu akbar.

With the elative the book ends: “tammat”, “it is finished”. In a few pages the student has built from faʿala every verb form and every derived noun of the sound triliteral. The next books of the Dars-i Niẓāmī take the weak verbs and the augmented patterns, on the same scale.

tasks.prompt: Build the masculine elative from yafʿulu, step by step, and say why it has no tanwīn.
tasks.answer: Drop the sign: fʿulu. Add the hamza: afʿul-. Give the ʿayn a fatḥa: afʿal-. No tanwīn: afʿalu. It is a diptote, an adjective with the pattern of a verb.

tasks.prompt: Build the feminine elative.
tasks.answer: Drop the sign, give the fāʾ a ḍamma, make the ʿayn quiescent, give the lām a fatḥa and join the short alif after it: fuʿlā.

tasks.prompt: Give the four forms of the feminine elative.
tasks.answer: Fuʿlā (singular), fuʿlayāni (dual), fuʿlayātun (sound plural), fuʿalun (broken plural).

text.original: فصل: این همه که گفته شد بحث اسم آله بود. چون خواهی که اسم تفضیل بنا کنی، علامت مضارع را حذف کن و همزه اسم تفضیل در اول او در آر، و عین کلمه را فتحه ده اگر مفتوح نباشد، و لام را تنوین ملحق مکن، و این طریق بنای اسم تفضیل مذکر است.
text.en: Section. All that has been said was on the noun of instrument. When you want to build the elative, drop the sign of the muḍāriʿ and bring in the hamza of the elative at its beginning; give the ʿayn of the word a fatḥa if it has none, and do not join tanwīn to the lām. This is the way of building the masculine elative.

text.original: اما چون صیغه مؤنث بنا کنی، بعد حذف علامت مضارع فا را ضمه ده و عین را ساکن کن و بعد لام الف مقصوره لاحق کن و لام کلمه را فتحه ده تا اسم تفضیل مؤنث گردد.
text.en: But when you build the feminine form, after dropping the sign of the muḍāriʿ give the fāʾ a ḍamma, make the ʿayn unvowelled, join the short alif (alif maqṣūra) after the lām and give the lām of the word a fatḥa, so that it becomes the feminine elative.

text.original:
أَفْعَلُ، أَفْعَلَانِ، أَفْعَلُونَ، أَفَاعِلُ
فُعْلَى، فُعْلَيَانِ، فُعْلَيَاتٌ، فُعَلٌ
تَمَّتْ
text.en:
afʿalu “doing more (m.)”, afʿalāni “two doing more (m.)”, afʿalūna “those doing more (m.)”, afāʿilu “those doing more (m., broken plural)”
fuʿlā “doing more (f.)”, fuʿlayāni “two doing more (f.)”, fuʿlayātun “those doing more (f.)”, fuʿalun “those doing more (f., broken plural)”
The end.
